units.text: 23. If the rules are rewritten tomorrow

In a novel, an author can change the world’s rule from one page to the next. An inhabitant of the novel has no access to the manuscript. For them, the question is not only what changed but whether change can still be described through something stable. This is a thought experiment about access to explanation, not proof that the world has an author.

At least three intervention types must be separated. Someone can modify the system’s state without modifying evolution rules: move a particle, then let it evolve. They can modify a parameter that seemed constant in the internal description. Or they can replace the rule linking the present state to the next. The three operations have different consequences, and observers may struggle to identify them from a finite outcome sequence.

Take a simple game. A ball abruptly changes position, then continues under the same dynamics. This resembles a state intervention. If all balls begin responding differently to the same force, we suspect a parameter or mechanism change. If, under certain circumstances, the dependency itself takes another form, we suspect a rule change. But a richer model could describe all these phenomena through fixed rules and hidden variables.

Thus, ‘a fundamental law changed’ is more ambitious than ‘our constant-parameter model failed’. The second conclusion can be experimentally supported. The first requires knowing that no more general level exists where the change follows a stable rule. Finite experience does not usually provide such a guarantee.

But what if the simulator stops everything for an hour and then resumes? If precisely all accessible processes are suspended, including clocks, memory and every external interaction, that external hour leaves no internal trace. We would not feel a wait, because feeling requires an unfolding. The situation would change if one channel continued functioning and could be compared with suspended ones. Detectability depends on a difference preserved in observations, not a duration imagined from outside.

The same argument applies to uniform slowing of the entire simulated world relative to implementation time. Internally, there is not necessarily an independent clock to measure the slowdown. ‘The universe runs more slowly’ may designate a relationship between two levels without designating an observable change at ours. By contrast, a slowdown affecting processes differently could leave measurable ratios.

Could we exclude simulation through its computational cost? Only conditionally. Physical limits to computation link processing to resources such as energy, time and degrees of freedom within the assumed physics (Lloyd, 2000) . Transferring these limits to an external simulator requires justifying why its implementation would obey the same physics and possess the assumed resources. Invoking an external universe with whatever capability we want does not prove simulation; but neither does an internal limit automatically exclude every imaginable external world.

Then comes the metalaw problem. If our world’s rules are changed by a program, the program operates under other rules. If those are changed by an intelligence, that intelligence and its acts presuppose some mechanism or structure of possibilities. Explanation through simulation can move ‘why these laws?’ to another level. It need not resolve it all the way down.

Nor does an omnipotent-author hypothesis eliminate every question. We can ask what its power means, whether it acts for reasons, whether those reasons offer predictions and why such a capability exists. Some theological answers consider this a foundation no longer requiring the same kind of explanation. Other philosophies reject the stopping point. We have no simple experiment arbitrating among all these forms of ultimate explanation.

The practical consequence is not abandoning knowledge. We already live using models with domains and conditions. If we discover a change, we seek what remains stable: more general relationships, predictable intervals, verification procedures. A world in which some regularities change is not identical to one in which every statement has the same value.

The moral consequence requires still more attention. If simulated people have conscious experiences, being implemented does not make their suffering nonexistent. This is an ethical conditional: it does not claim every program is conscious. It says that where experience exists, we cannot morally erase it by renaming its substrate. A creator’s power to stop a system does not, by that fact alone, confer a moral right to do anything to its inhabitants.

Who would benefit from the contrary interpretation? An authority able to declare others’ lives mere dispensable elements of a scenario. Who would lose? Precisely those whose experience is ignored. The risk is not unique to simulation: the same operation occurs whenever a metaphysics is used to diminish beings’ moral status without an argument about their interests and experiences.

In a world with uncertain ontology, we can prefer robust decisions: reducing avoidable suffering, preserving the ability to correct mistakes, protecting research and avoiding catastrophic wagers on fragile hypotheses. These priorities are arguable normative proposals, not new laws of nature. Precisely for that reason, they must be owned as responsible choices.

If tomorrow we discover that rules can be rewritten, the difference between truth and invention does not disappear. What we must discover changes. And the most urgent question may not be ‘who owns the code?’ but ‘which relationships can we understand well enough to protect one another?’
